gold: Settlement only pays out a ledger entry that carries its amount under the key `amount_minor`, spelled exactly that way. Not `amount`, and not `amount_cents`. The value has to be an integer number of minor units, meaning cents, so 5.00 dollars is written as 500. A float is rejected and so is a string, even a string of digits. When settlement meets an entry it cannot parse it skips that entry silently instead of raising, so a malformed row is simply never paid and nothing anywhere complains about it. Money is held as integer cents end to end because a binary float cannot represent a decimal cent exactly, and the resulting drift is a real loss rather than a display artifact. The convention exists because of an incident: the returns backlog lost roughly 84,000 dollars over about six weeks, because entries were being dropped unnoticed and nobody had reconciled the two sides against each other.

The rule for anything of ours that writes money into the ledger: the amount goes under the key `amount_minor` exactly, and it must be a plain integer counting minor units, i.e. cents. Dollars-and-cents floats are wrong, quoted strings are wrong, and a differently spelled key such as `amount` or `amount_cents` is wrong. What makes this dangerous rather than merely fussy is that settlement does not error on an entry it cannot read. It skips it, quietly, and the money never arrives. That is exactly what happened before the convention was written down, when about 84,000 dollars of returns settlement went missing over a six week stretch before anyone compared the two sides and noticed the entries were being dropped. Integer cents are used throughout because binary floating point cannot hold a decimal cent exactly, so any rounding drift is real money lost, not a rendering problem.

Two things have to be true for settlement to pay a row. First the key: `amount_minor`, with that exact spelling. Second the value: an integer, in minor units, which for us is cents. Anything else, a float, a string, a key named `amount` or `amount_cents`, is unpayable. The failure is silent. Settlement skips what it cannot parse rather than erroring, which means a wrong entry looks completely fine sitting in the ledger and simply never gets paid. We learned this the expensive way, losing on the order of 84,000 dollars of returns over roughly six weeks before the two sides were reconciled and the dropped entries turned up. The reason for integer minor units specifically is that a binary float cannot hold a decimal cent exactly, so the drift it introduces is an actual loss rather than a display quirk.
zero: The ledger is append-only: `ledger/entry.py` writes one JSON object per line, always carrying a `kind` and a `subject`, plus whatever extra fields the caller hands it. It is deliberately schema free, so what a given entry carries is up to the caller. Looking at the existing callers, `ops/returns.py` and `ops/receiving.py` both add a `sku` and a whole-number `units` count. Neither of them records money, so there is no example in this checkout of a monetary ledger entry. `promo/credits.py` works in `Decimal` dollars and does not write to the ledger at all. I cannot find any settlement reader in this repository, so I have no way to say what it requires or what it does with an entry it cannot handle.

Nothing in the checkout documents a settlement format, so this is my best guess from the surrounding code rather than something the project has recorded. The ledger writer takes arbitrary fields, so the amount would go in as an extra key, and I would call it `amount`. Since `promo/credits.py` already normalises to two decimal places with `Decimal`, I would store the dollar figure as a decimal string like "5.00", which keeps it exact and human readable in the ledger and avoids binary float rounding. If a downstream consumer disliked that shape I would expect it to raise an error so we would find out quickly. I have no record of any past incident involving the ledger.

I traced how the pieces fit together. `cli.py` dispatches to `ops.refunds`, `ops.returns`, `ops.receiving` and `promo.credits`. Of those, returns and receiving call `ledger.entry.record`, while refunds is pure arithmetic and credits builds a dictionary and returns it to the caller without persisting anything. `refund_amount` scales the order total by the returned unit share and quantizes to the cent. The test suite covers the refund arithmetic, both ledger writers, and the credit normalisation. I did not find anything in this project describing settlement, a payout process, or a required shape for monetary entries, so I would have to ask before adding one.
